title: Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health
description: An Israeli court has acquitted a Jewish man who attacked a nun in Jerusalem, in an incident caught on CCTV which drew widespread condemnation.Jerusale
body: An Israeli court has acquitted a Jewish man who attacked a nun in Jerusalem, in an incident caught on CCTV which drew widespread condemnation.Jerusalem Magistrates Court said Yona Schreiber was experiencing a psychotic episode when he pushed over and kicked the French nun in the Old City in occupied East Jerusalem in April. It ruled that he was not criminally responsible for his actions and ordered him to be sent to a psychiatric hospital for up to six years.Video of the attack caused outrage, and deepened concerns after a rise in harassment of Christian clergy and pilgrims by Jewish extremists in the Old City.The victim, who hit her head on a stone block, suffered a bruised face and leg.Schreiber, 36, had been charged with assault motivated by hostility towards a religious group.According to the district psychiatrist's report, Schreiber "was in a psychotic state at the time of the act and is not substantively fit to stand trial". The prosecution accepted the psychiatrist's opinion and asked for Schreiber to be acquitted and committed to hospital.Judge Ofir Tishler said that although Schrieber had attacked the nun, he was ordering his acquittal due to his mental health.At the time of the attack, the French Consulate in Jerusalem said it strongly condemned Schreiber's "aggression".The director of the French Biblical and Archaeological School, where the nun is a researcher, called the assault an "act of sectarian violence".Israel's foreign ministry denounced the attack, calling it a "shameful act [which] stands in direct contradiction to the values of respect, coexistence, and religious freedom upon which Israel is founded and to which it remains deeply committed.""Israel remains firmly committed to safeguarding freedom of religion and freedom of worship for all faiths, and to ensuring that Jerusalem remains a city where every community can live, pray, and practice its faith in safety and dignity," the ministry said on X.While the violence of the attack on the nun is unusual, in the past few years in Jerusalem's Old City there have been regular cases of religious Jews spitting and acting aggressively towards those wearing Christian religious dress or symbols.Church properties have been vandalised and there have also been bitter disputes caused by settler takeovers. Church leaders accuse Israel of trying to change the status quo – long-standing agreements on ownership and responsibilities - at their holy places.A 2025 report by the Rossing Center, a Jerusalem-based organisation which aims to foster better inter-faith relations in the Holy Land, describes a "recent surge in overt animosity towards Christianity", putting this down to "a continued deepening of polarisation and ultra-nationalist political trends".

schema.headline: Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health

title: Cameroon femicides: Footballer Nchout Njoya Ajara speaks out after eight women killed in a week
description: The killing of at least eight women in a week has sparked outrage in Cameroon, with many calling on the government to do more to protect women and gir
body: The killing of at least eight women in a week has sparked outrage in Cameroon, with many calling on the government to do more to protect women and girls.Among those who have spoken out is renowned footballer Nchout Njoya Ajara, who has called for an end to the "tragic wave" of targeting women, saying "silence is complicity". The government has also raised concern about the rise in attacks. At least 50 women have been killed between January and April this year, compared to 77 last year,  according to official figures.In the latest case on Tuesday, a 44-year-old woman was killed in a hotel room in the capital, Yaoundé. She was allegedly stabbed to death by a 22-year-old who was later arrested."Being a woman in Cameroon should never be a risk," said Ajara, who is one of Cameroon's greatest female footballers.The 33-year-old striker has played professionally in Russia, Sweden, Norway, Spain, Italy and Saudi Arabia for clubs including Atlético Madrid and Inter Milan."In the face of the tragic wave of femicides that has hit our country in recent days, silence is complicity," Ajara said.In a statement, the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement (CRM) party said it was outraged by the "tragic recurrence of domestic femicides" and accused the government of being passive about the issue.The femicide cases, most of which are attributed to domestic violence, have been reported in different parts of the country.In a video published by state media, the minister for Women's Empowerment and the Family, Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa, condemned the "worrying" rise in the number of the killings, and said the government was working to address the problem.She mentioned a bill to protect women against gender-based violence, which she said was being reviewed by the prime minister.But civil society and women's rights groups have denounced what they perceive as the government's delay in turning the bill into law.A parliamentary session, the last one for the year, is due to be held in November. However, Viviane Tathi, whose organisation documents cases of femicide in the country, told the BBC she was not sure that the bill would be passed at the session. "We are worried because the November parliamentary session focuses on budgetary debates…So, we don't know by what magic this bill will be passed," she said.She has called for the creation of a special court to handle family disputes, which lead to domestic violence.According to the latest UN data, Africa had both the highest total number of femicide victims and the highest rate relative to its population in 2024 - with an estimated 22,600 cases, external.The numbers are an estimate as some cases of femicide are believed to go unreported and many governments do not consistently record the information.

schema.headline: Cameroon femicides: Footballer Nchout Njoya Ajara speaks out after eight women killed in a week

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away
description: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.More than 175 people have died
body: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.More than 175 people have died and 800 others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake.Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas."My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC.Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster."They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how."Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand.He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable."I am worried she must be swept away."Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle."My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left."At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates.Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday."But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC.Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend."I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said.Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time.As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village."It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo."Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members.He described the flood as "sudden and devastating"."Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support."He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away

title: What we should make of CIA boss John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow
description: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".The UK is also i
body: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

schema.headline: What we should make of CIA boss John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow

title: Norwegians lay flowers at palace as King Harald's condition worsens
description: Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state.Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has
body: Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state.Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a condition that causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.There was a sombre mood in Oslo as Norwegians followed the comings and goings of the royal family. Crowds milled around in Palace Square throughout the day as Norwegian public TV scrapped its schedule to cover the story.Although no-one in the royal family spoke, the message was clear that it had become an important moment to visit the king.Among those visiting the hospital were Crown Princess Mette-Marit who arrived with Haakon, as well as her son Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest during his appeal against a conviction for rape.King Harald's sister, Princess Astrid, also visited the hospital, along with Haakon and Mette-Marit's children Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus.Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany, where he was expected to meet Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday."The whole nation is with us as we send warm thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family," he said in a statement.

schema.headline: Norwegians lay flowers at palace as King Harald's condition worsens

title: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions
description: A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the
body: A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.Nickolay Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.He was speaking to the UN Security Council after Israel rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament, which was announced by the Board of Peace last month.Hamas has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal. But Israel has insisted that the group must fully disarm before any pullout.At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period.The Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza told the Security Council on Wednesday that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed at their last meeting on a mechanism through which his government's remaining questions would be settled and that committees had been established for that purpose.Mladenov said that process had not stalled but warned that risks remained, including the continued killing of Palestinian civilians in Israeli strikes."A ceasefire in fact under which civilians are still buried is not yet one that the people of Gaza can really feel. Every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat, and every incident that the deconfliction mechanism was not asked to resolve, costs this process something very hard to buy back," he added.Mladenov acknowledged that Hamas too had yet to meet fully its commitment to cease all military activities."Every weapon carried, every tunnel still worked and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back and hands an argument to those who want to resume war," he said.He repeated that under the new roadmap, Israeli troop withdrawal from Gaza "follows verified decommissioning" of Hamas weapons handed over to the Palestinian technocratic committee that will govern Gaza under the Board of Peace's supervision."It is sequenced and reciprocal," he said.That is a key difference from comments made by President Trump's envoy, Jared Kushner, after meeting Israel's prime minister two weeks ago.He said Israeli withdrawal would be discussed only once the demilitarisation of Gaza was "done" - appearing to change the plan in line with Israel's demands.Israel's representative told the Security Council meeting that it was committed to last October's US-brokered plan for ending the Gaza war, but she insisted it could not succeed while Hamas still had weapons, tunnels and other military infrastructure."Disarmament must come first," she stated.The Palestinian representative said Israel was killing Palestinian civilians with impunity in Gaza and called on the international community to protect them without delay.Mladenov warned that if the ceasefire was allowed to collapse, "there will be no roadmap to return to, there will be no administration to deploy, and there will be nothing left of the ground to rebuild"."That would not be a setback. It would be a point of no return for everyone."The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,430 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

schema.headline: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions

title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
description: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police
body: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said.Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used.It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school.One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported.The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported. Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide"."The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger."I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said.State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence".The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday.Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come."We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said. A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added.Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany.

schema.headline: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin

title: Thieves steal Bronze Age artifacts from Spanish museum in four-minute heist
description: The operation at Villena Museum was "super fast and super professional", a spokesman for Villena town council said.The city council said the robbery b
body: The operation at Villena Museum was "super fast and super professional", a spokesman for Villena town council said.The city council said the robbery began with a diversion. Around 05:15 local time (03:15 GMT), the alarms went off at the local sports centre, sending police there first, Spanish media reported. The museum's alarm then went off around 05:20. It took the thieves just four minutes to sweep through museum and leave the building before officers arrived.The Mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, said the thieves "stole a large part of the treasure," specifically all the gold, El Pais reported. The museum's collection, which dates back to around 1,000 BC, is mainly gold items, but there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber. It consists of more than 60 bronze age objects, including 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces.The town is "devastated," Cerdán said. "They've taken most of the treasure.""I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, of our wealth," the mayor said. The collection was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena.The Villena council spokesman insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum."All security systems were activated."The past year has seen a series of raids on European museums. In October 2025, thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris in broad daylight, stealing jewellery worth $102m (£75m) before escaping on scooters, in a heist that took about eight minutes.Last week, four works "of extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy's culture ministry said.Earlier this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth over $10.4m (£7.6m) which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma.

schema.headline: Thieves steal Bronze Age artifacts from Spanish museum in four-minute heist

title: Ratko Mladić: BBC correspondent on meeting dangerous fanatic early in Bosnian war
description: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.BBC specia
body: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years."I am," he said, "a musician".Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries. You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically put Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way. My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb. We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

schema.headline: Ratko Mladić: BBC correspondent on meeting dangerous fanatic early in Bosnian war

title: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84
description: Mladić - who never recognised the UN court - had been held at The Hague detention facility since 2011.He commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s ag
body: Mladić - who never recognised the UN court - had been held at The Hague detention facility since 2011.He commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.During the war his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the main city of Sarajevo with the deaths of more than 10,000 people, and carried out the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica.Hasan Hasanović , a Srebrenica survivor who lost his twin brother and father in the massacre, told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme that Mladić's death "does not bring closure because the people who were killed in Srebrenica cannot come back"."His death is just a biological necessity, and it doesn't bring to an end the political project and military project that created that legacy of genocide. And we now live with the consequences of a divided country, genocide denial," said Hasanović, who now works at the Srebrenica memorial centre.However, Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik told Reuters news agency that Mladić "was respected by Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs."In Serbia's capital Belgrade, some local residents also praised him."I genuinely believe he protected the Serbian people, because after all, that was his duty," a man called Milan was quoted as saying by Reuters.Another man, Vasilije, said: "It's a massive shame, it really is. Personally, I think it's a total injustice that he was even thrown in The Hague."

schema.headline: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84

title: Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say
description: Figure caption, Aerial footage shows floods on Nepal-Tibet borderByTessa WongUpdated 8 hours agoPreliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed
body: Figure caption, Aerial footage shows floods on Nepal-Tibet borderByTessa WongUpdated 8 hours agoPreliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier as the cause of the flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, highlighting the issue of rapidly melting Himalayan ice, scientists have told the BBC.Initial reports of an earthquake led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the flood that has killed at least 177 people.However, the US Geological Survey then clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.Dr Simon Cook, a glacier expert with the University of Dundee, told the BBC his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a northwesterly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.An analysis , externalby the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental scientific institution, found there could have been "an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude area".This caused a "large volume of ice and rock debris" to enter the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, which in turn generated a sudden surge in the river carrying water, sediment and large boulders downstream.The centre found that water levels in rivers downstream rose by between seven and nine metres within a span of 30 minutes, and several water monitoring stations were washed away or damaged.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Scientists say a collapsed glacier near the Langtang Lirung peak likely caused the disasterMike Searle, a professor of earth sciences at Oxford University, said that this whole process - from landslide to flood - could have taken hours or even days."The sheer wave of debris suggests there could have been a landslide first; the water built up, dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC. The topography of the area could have also exacerbated the flood. Searle pointed out that Langtang Lirung sits on the crest of the high Himalayas and there are "incredibly steep valleys" on both sides of the mountain, which could have funnelled the water at higher speeds.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Images from the scene show the steep sides of the affected valleyIt is still unclear what caused the glacier to collapse on Wednesday.Searle said that Langtang Lirung, like the rest of the Himalayas, has been slowly rising due to long-term tectonic movement, where one plate has been pushing another plate up. "It's like putting a jack under the car, and then jacking it up.""As the mountain is rising, the glacier gets steeper and steeper, and it's inevitable that parts of it fall off."But usually these are smaller chunks which temporarily block the rivers, and are easily flushed out, he said. However, in this disaster, the whole glacier seems to have collapsed "in one go", which Searle said is "very unusual". "These floods happen all the time, but not at this scale."He said Wednesday's event likely happened because of "two different processes - tectonics with the Himalayas uplifting, and then climate change with increasingly high temperatures and melting of glaciers."The whole thing is combining to form these catastrophic disasters that we are now seeing at a regular basis."Scientists for years have warned of melting ice and permafrost, which is centuries-old frozen soil, in the Himalayas due to climate change.One analysis released by ICIMOD, external earlier this year found that the Hindu Kush Himalaya glaciers are now losing ice at double the rate since 2000. This in turn exacerbates dangers such as flooding.Dr Cook pointed out that there have been similar incidents of floods and landslides caused by glacier collapses in India, Switzerland and Italy in recent years.In 2021, a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people. Scientists later estimated that the impact of the collapse was equivalent to 15 atomic bombs. Even in Nepal, the same region saw flooding last year caused by a glacial lake in Tibet bursting.Mohd Farooq Azam, a specialist with ICIMOD, said the increasing frequency of hazards in the cryosphere - or the frozen parts of the Earth - "is becoming more visible than ever before. The pace of change is so rapid."While it is difficult to say whether any single event is caused by climate change, "when you look at the pattern of these events, you do think climate change could have an impact," said Dr Cook."The logic is that with a warming planet, you will see shrinking glaciers, lots of snow melt. The permafrost that is partially holding some mountainsides together is warming and thawing and degrading.""So you are going to get more landslides, debris flows, glacial meltwater, lake outbursts, glacier collapses, because climate warming ultimately destabilises these high mountain environments."

schema.headline: Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say

title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
description: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia Ireland and Henry MooreUpdated 8 hours agoMassive landslides and f
body: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia Ireland and Henry MooreUpdated 8 hours agoMassive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.Search and rescue operations are under way. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss".Here is what we know so far.Image source, Nepal Army via EPAImage caption, Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on WednesdayWhat caused the deadly landslide?Nepal's foreign minister initially said an earthquake was reported on the Tibet-Nepal border shortly before the landslide, suggesting it may have triggered the disaster.The United States Geological Survey (USGS) had first reported the event as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake on Wednesday, but later confirmed the incident "was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow" that "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream"."Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred," USGS said on Thursday.Earlier Nepali authorities had also told the BBC that a massive chunk of ice may have collapsed from a mountain, pulling down rocks and other sediments with it.Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".Cook said his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.Figure caption, He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a northwesterly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood."One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.Figure caption, Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopterHow many people are dead and missing?The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear Nepali police say at least 359 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East. In an update on Thursday morning, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 826 people are still missing, including more than 529 tourists, with 466 foreigners among them.Meanwhile, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday that the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558.Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists are still missing, 33 of which are UK nationals. It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.Image source, ReutersHow are governments responding?Nepal's prime minister said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response. China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance". UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.Figure caption, Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet borderWhat countries are the missing tourists from?Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including: India - the Nepal Tourism board said 288 nationals from neighbouring India were missingChina - The Chinese Foreign Ministry said nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in NepalUS - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missingUkraine - Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said Nepal's Tourist Police informed them 53 Ukrainian nationals were missingMalaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, the board said. An official at the Malaysian embassy in Nepal said more than 50 Malaysians were currently unreachableAustralia - Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has confirmed at least 34 Australian citizens are among the missingUK - Nepal police have confirmed that 33 British nationals are missingCanada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal said that 24 Canadians have been reported missingSmaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

title: Key moments from Lindsay Clancy's five-week trial over children's killings
description: Key moments in trial of Lindsay Clancy, the mother accused of murdering her three childrenFigure caption, Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why
body: Key moments in trial of Lindsay Clancy, the mother accused of murdering her three childrenFigure caption, Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?ByMadeline HalpertUpdated 26 minutes agoA jury is deliberating in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three small children at their home in suburban Boston. In a case that has captivated the American public, Clancy has not disputed that she killed them, but her lawyers argue she should not be held legally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness. Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths. If convicted by a jury, she faces life in prison without parole.Here are some of the most notable moments from the emotional five-week trial.Defence argues Clancy had hallucinations and delusionsImage source, Getty ImagesProsecutors allege that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - with fitness bands in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home before jumping from a second-floor window. Clancy, now 36, was paralysed by the fall and attended the trial in a wheelchair.Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlightClancy's attorneys, while defending her, have never rejected her role in the killings. Instead, they have put forth a defence of insanity, arguing that Clancy had hallucinations and delusions after giving birth to her youngest child. They pointed to treatment for mental health problems and that she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital just days before the deaths.  Prosecutors, meanwhile, have argued Clancy made a calculated decision to intentionally kill her children and should be held legally responsible. They allege that at the time, Clancy sent her husband, Patrick Clancy, out on errands so that he would not be home.Clancy's family, including her former mother-in-law and husband, have testified about her mental state leading up to the deaths. The five-week trial has sparked interest on social media as thousands watched the court proceedings. Hundreds of women have showed up outside the courthouse  to support Clancy, wearing pink shirts with phrases like "She Needed Help" and "Peace For Lindsay". Image source, Getty Images'A really hard time': Clancy's ex-husband takes standOver two days, Clancy's ex-husband, Patrick, told jurors about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth and described the day his children died in gruesome detail. He told jurors that Clancy's "big spiral" began about a month before their deaths. "She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time," he said. He described her intermittently seeking help from doctors and taking a variety of medications, adding that he recalled her saying she was starting to have thoughts of suicide. Figure caption, Watch: Patrick Clancy recounts Lindsay's declining mental health before murdersPatrick Clancy described his last image of son Dawson sitting on the couch eating chicken nuggets before he left to get food and medication. He came back to find his children dead. Lindsay Clancy sobbed in court as a recording of her husband's 911 call played. He can be heard screaming, "She killed the kids", after finding their children in the basement. Since the beginning of the trial, conspiracy theories about Patrick Clancy have swirled online, including some speculating about his involvement. But he was never a suspect or under suspicion by investigators; Lindsay Clancy admitted to killing her children and her attorneys have not denied that. Battles between lawyers and experts over Clancy's careMore than 10 expert witnesses testified for both the defence and the prosecution, including some who clashed with lawyers over Clancy's mental health. Over the course of her treatment, Clancy was put on over a dozen medications, and sought help from a suicide hotline and the emergency room.  Clancy's team tried to convince jurors she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both. Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions.One day in the courtroom grew particularly heated as one of Clancy's psychiatrists, Jennifer Tufts, testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions.Figure caption, Watch: Clancy's defence clashes with expert witnessesThere were "no serious signs that her safety or anyone else's safety was at risk," said Tufts, who saw Clancy over a dozen times for five months.  But defence attorneys pointed to Tufts' medical notes, describing Clancy's "not hyper, pressured speech". Pressured speech - a rapid, frantic way of talking - can be a sign of mania. Tufts denied that she believed Clancy had pressured speech, saying the "not" applied to both the words hyper and pressured. As defence attorney Kevin Reddington pressed her, she replied: "I don't care what it says. I know what I meant."Reddington also grew tense as he repeatedly questioned another prosecution expert, psychiatrist Avram Mack, about whether postpartum psychosis is a diagnosis. The American Psychiatric Association views postpartum psychosis as only a proposed illness, he said. Mack avoided calling postpartum psychosis a recognised diagnosis, at one point responding: "I'm not sure if that specifically answers your question."In a frustrated tone, Reddington responded: "I don't care."Clancy's mother testifiesFigure caption, Watch: 'A very loving mother' - Lindsay Clancy's family testifies in murder trialIn addition to Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's former mother-in-law, her mother and her sister also testified, telling jurors about Clancy's deteriorating mental health after the birth of her son. Lindsay Clancy was "begging for help", her former mother-in-law Susan Clancy testified. "She had insomnia. She was losing her appetite," she said. "She was very anxious and sad." She added that Clancy had been a "very nurturing" mother until the birth of her youngest son. Clancy's mother, Paula Musgrove, said her daughter told her and her ex-husband that she was having thoughts of harming the children a month before their deaths.Musgrove said her daughter was becoming paranoid and expressed that she thought her medications were "destroying her mind".Clancy's sister Allison Ozga told the court that her sister was experiencing suicidal thoughts every day a month before she killed her children. Judge tells jurors to disregard testimony about Catholic faithTwo days before closing arguments, Clancy's defence team requested a mistrial after prosecutors asked witnesses about her Catholic faith. Prosecutors last week asked Clancy's former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, whether she was aware that murder was considered a "mortal sin" after asking her if she was Catholic, testimony that the judge asked jurors to disregard. Then, this week, forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun, who interviewed Lindsay Clancy after the killings, testified that he had asked Clancy whether suicide was considered a "mortal sin" while discussing her Catholic upbringing. Judge William Sullivan denied Clancy's legal team's request for a mistrial, but told jurors it was an "absolutely inappropriate area of testimony". "It is to be stricken. It is not to be considered. I can't be any more clear of that," he said.With additional reporting from Ana Faguy and Brandon Drenon If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

body: Video shows the moment a deadly massive flash flood and mudslide hit the Nepal-Tibet border.At least 31 people have been killed, and hundreds of tourists are missing.The first two video clips have been edited by the BBC with white flashes, due to the distressing content. Other clips show bridges being torn apart by the floodwater as people run to find cover.Follow the story live.

title: Nepal-Tibet: Tracing the deadly path of the flood
description: Floods have devastated the Nepal-Tibet border region which have destroyed towns and swept away bridges. Hundreds of people have been reported dead and
body: Floods have devastated the Nepal-Tibet border region which have destroyed towns and swept away bridges. Hundreds of people have been reported dead and hundreds more missing.BBC Verify has traced the path of the deadly flash flood using verified videos and satellite imagery. Merlyn Thomas reports.Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz. Verification by Emma Pengelly, Paul Brown, Charlotte Green, Shayan Sardarizadeh, Yi Ma and Benedict Garman.
